title: In the battle of the AI stacks, model quality won’t be the most decisive factor
gist: In the US-China AI stack competition in emerging markets, especially Africa, the decisive variables are chips, data centers, energy, cloud regions, financing, and recipient-state absorptive capacity — not model benchmark scores. Kenya's stalled $1bn Microsoft/G42 data center and South Africa's regulatory failures show projects die at the infrastructure and governance layer, while China's Digital Silk Road and cheap open-weight models (Qwen overtook Llama on Hugging Face) exploit an already-installed terrestrial stack.

insights.claim: In the US-China AI stack contest in emerging markets, state capacity and infrastructure deals will prove more decisive than model quality, because the contest hinges on chips, data centers, energy, cloud regions, and the financing that binds them together with recipient states' ability to regulate, procure, and absorb what is offered.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Points investors toward power, permitting, fiber, and financing exposure rather than model-layer IP when underwriting emerging-market AI buildouts.
insights.quote: Topping the model leaderboards may count for less than the ability to finance, power, and permit the infrastructure stack underneath the models.
insights.locator: In the contest between US and Chinese artificial intelligence stacks

insights.claim: At the point of adoption model quality is increasingly fungible, because for many public-sector and enterprise use cases in emerging markets both American and Chinese stacks are good enough and China's open-weight, low-cost offerings can offset whatever performance gap remains.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Model-performance leadership does not translate into emerging-market share; pricing and bundled financing do.
insights.quote: Model performance has converged sufficiently that infrastructure and deployment constraints matter more.
insights.locator: The decisive layer

insights.claim: The bottom of the AI stack is not easily swappable — chips clear export licensing or they do not, data centers get financed, powered and permitted or they stall, cloud regions anchor to long-term procurement or they collapse — and dependency once installed is sticky because switching costs sit in infrastructure rather than software.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: First-mover infrastructure wins in a market compound into decade-long lock-in; early cloud-region and fiber positions are the durable asset.
insights.quote: the switching costs sit in the infrastructure layer more so than software
insights.locator: But the bottom of the stack is not so easily swappable

themes.theme: Chinese open weights as default developer foundation

insights.claim: By late 2025 Alibaba's Qwen family of open-weight models had overtaken Meta's Llama as the most downloaded model family on Hugging Face, and Chinese models accounted for more than 45 percent of downloads among leading open models.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Developer mindshare is a leading indicator of enterprise deployment; Meta losing the open-model default undercuts a core plank of its AI strategy.
insights.locator: By late 2025, Qwen, the family of open-weight models

insights.claim: The strategic significance of Chinese open models is not that they are universally better than American alternatives but that they are becoming the default foundations on which developers around the world choose to build.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Default-foundation status creates ecosystem gravity (tooling, fine-tunes, talent) that benchmark parity alone cannot reverse.
insights.locator: The significance is less that Chinese models are universally better

insights.claim: At the model layer Chinese platforms such as DeepSeek R1 and Qwen compete on cost and open weights instead of peak capability, a formula well suited to capturing emerging-market share.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Price-led open-weight competition compresses the addressable API market for US closed-model vendors outside the OECD.
insights.locator: At the model layer, Chinese platforms such as DeepSeek R1

themes.theme: Washington's export machinery reveals its own assumptions

insights.claim: The American AI Exports Program encourages industry consortia to offer integrated AI stacks backed by licensing support, financing, and advocacy, and its spring call for proposals mandated five stack layers from AI-optimized hardware and cloud/network infrastructure through sector applications such as healthcare and agriculture.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: US-backed consortium financing is a live procurement channel; vendors that can assemble a full five-layer stack qualify for licensing and advocacy support.
insights.locator: What Washington is doing

insights.claim: The US call for proposals presumes a package satisfies the content test if American value accounts for at least 51 percent of the hardware layer, requires a model's intellectual property to be majority American-owned and free of country-of-concern control, and where a package relies on open-weight models requires an American firm to supply integration, fine-tuning, security, and support.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A concrete 51 percent domestic-content threshold that shapes which hardware and integration vendors can be included in US-backed export consortia.
insights.locator: The design of the government’s call is also instructive

insights.claim: Nothing in the US designation criteria measures how good the models are, and none of the export machinery would exist if Washington believed model quality alone won markets.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: US policy has already conceded that distribution and financing, not benchmarks, decide market share — read policy design as revealed preference.
insights.quote: Nothing in the designation criteria measures how good the models are, and none of this export machinery would exist if Washington believed model quality alone won markets.
insights.locator: Nothing in the designation criteria measures

insights.claim: The US call for proposals barred country-of-concern firms from any layer of a designated consortium, and Commerce told applicants that a proposal is stronger where American engagement can tip a procuring entity choosing between American technology and technology from a country of concern.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Full-stack exclusion rules force emerging-market buyers into an either/or bloc choice, raising the value of early vendor relationships.
insights.locator: The call for proposals barred country-of-concern firms

themes.theme: China's Digital Silk Road head start

insights.claim: China's Digital Silk Road paired state-backed finance with exports of the Chinese stack to governments across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East, with Huawei Cloud marketing integrated cloud-and-AI packages in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and North Africa and embedding itself deeply in Thailand's digital infrastructure plus Malaysia and Indonesia.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Chinese AI distribution rides pre-existing cloud contracts; displacement requires replacing infrastructure, not just offering a better model.
insights.locator: But Beijing acted first

insights.claim: The terrestrial layer across much of Africa is already Chinese-dominant — Chinese-built network equipment, affordable handsets through firms such as Transsion, and digital-payments infrastructure — so Chinese AI services arrive as an increment rather than a new installation.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Incremental-cost advantage means Chinese AI can be bundled into installed telecom and payments rails at near-zero customer acquisition cost.
insights.locator: The terrestrial layer is already dominant across much of Africa

insights.claim: Huawei displaced established competitors Nokia and Ericsson to become a leading telecommunications infrastructure supplier in Africa using vendor finance, integrated infrastructure packages, and rapid deployment rather than overwhelming technical superiority — and the emerging AI stack contest resembles that earlier competition.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The telecom precedent is the base rate: vendor financing beats technical superiority in emerging markets, a bearish read for Western AI vendors without concessional finance.
insights.locator: This pattern has appeared in Africa before

themes.theme: State capacity as the binding constraint

insights.claim: Microsoft's planned one-billion-dollar data center in Kenya with Emirati national champion G42 stalled after the Kenyan government balked at the long-term fiscal guarantees and energy infrastructure commitments needed to anchor the project — the technology and capital were available but the state's absorptive ability was not.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Announced emerging-market data center capex should be discounted heavily for sovereign guarantee and grid risk; Kenya is the worked example.
insights.quote: Once a project is blocked at the infrastructure layer, improvements in model quality become largely immaterial.
insights.locator: African outcomes turn on state capacity

insights.claim: South Africa has kept Starlink out for years over local-ownership rules and withdrew its own draft national AI policy in April after the draft was found to contain fabricated citations suspected of being AI-generated.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Regulatory design decides market entry and regulatory capacity decides whether a strategy exists at all — both are underpriced risks in African tech expansion plans.
insights.quote: Regulatory design decides which providers may enter; regulatory capacity decides whether the state can even articulate a strategy of its own.
insights.locator: Or consider South Africa

insights.claim: Nigeria, Kenya, and other African nations increasingly frame AI through the language of sovereignty, resilience, and strategic autonomy, and the sixty-billion-dollar Africa AI Fund announced at the 2025 Global AI Summit on Africa targets infrastructure, talent, and startup development ahead of frontier model creation.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A $60bn pool explicitly aimed at infrastructure and talent, not model R&D — the addressable spend is in power, data centers, and skills, not frontier labs.
insights.locator: Across the continent, the sovereignty agenda

insights.claim: Emerging-market data centers will succeed where there is energy flexibility, coordinated permitting, and workforce pipelines, with structural risk concentrated in grid redundancy, pricing volatility, and uneven regulation.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A three-factor screen (energy flexibility, permitting coordination, workforce) for ranking which emerging markets can actually host AI capacity.
insights.locator: Emerging-market data centers will succeed where

themes.theme: Cassava as the template for who can execute

insights.claim: The NVIDIA-Cassava partnership, a reported $720-million program, is rolling out NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure across South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt, and Morocco, starting with three thousand GPUs at a South African facility and twelve thousand planned across the remaining markets over three to four years.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Concrete, sized African GPU demand — 15,000 GPUs over three to four years — and a named channel partner for Nvidia's Africa exposure.
insights.locator: The same emphasis is visible in the private sector

insights.claim: The Cassava deal was possible because Cassava, founded by Zimbabwean entrepreneur Strive Masiyiwa, already owned the scarce assets — a fiber network stretching from Cape Town to Cairo, data centers, and a renewable-energy business.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The winners in emerging-market AI are incumbent owners of fiber, land, and power, not model vendors — screen for that asset combination.
insights.locator: It was possible because Cassava

themes.theme: The caveat: frontier divergence would invert the thesis

insights.claim: If model capability diverges sharply again at the frontier through agentic systems with large productivity differentials, the assumption that models are largely interchangeable weakens and access to the most capable models could matter more than avoiding lock-in to any single stack.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The explicit kill-switch on the infrastructure-first thesis: watch agentic productivity differentials as the signal to re-rate model-layer exposure.
insights.quote: For now, the evidence points the other way, but that holds only under current conditions, and may not hold forever.
insights.locator: There is a caveat, though

insights.claim: The open question is whether the American AI Exports Program's consortium-and-financing model can win in states where the true bottleneck is procurement capacity, energy systems, and regulatory institutions, and what investing in those institutions ahead of the stack itself would do.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Suggests institutional capacity-building, not hardware subsidies, is the higher-leverage US intervention — a possible pivot in US development-finance policy.
